utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue, I would first like to give the reasons for the decisions of last Friday. Reasons for the decision on protective measures for the Witnesses 84, 239, and 270. The Prosecution's motion for protective measures for Witnesses 84, 239, and 270 was filed on the 12th of April, 2005. It was then amended on the 14th of April in relation to Witness 270 only. Also on the 14th of April, the Chamber invited the Defence to consider whether it might not concede the Prosecution's motion, in which case it would have avoided a time-consuming written submission, seeing that, in the first place, the applicable law on the subject of protective measures has been restated by this Chamber time and again, in what we think are very clear terms. Secondly, the Prosecution's motion seemed to make a relatively strong case in favour of protective measures for the three witnesses. While it is of no consequence, I note that at the time that we made our invitation to the Defence, only at that time we were informed of the Prosecution's further request to amend its motion in relation to Witness 270. But that development did not make any difference to the Chamber's invitation. The Defence reply to the motion was sent to the Chamber by e-mail on the afternoon of the 15th of April. The registrar has since kindly been asked to have it filed. The Defence did not fully concede the motion. More accurately, it opposed the motion, conceding for each witness some measure of privacy or protection, but not the measures requested. The Chamber deliberated on that same afternoon, following which the parties were informed by the legal officer of the Chamber's decision. The decision was to grant the motion as amended. I shall now summarise the reasons. In relation to Witnesses 84 and 239, both of whom are expected to allege that they were raped, it seems that the perpetrators of the alleged rapes are at large, or might still be at large. The question is whether the two witnesses should be granted voice distortion, image distortion, and pseudonyms which I will call the basic measures, in addition to private session for all testimony about the alleged rapes. The latter measure is not opposed by the Defence. The Chamber holds that the basic measures should be granted for both witnesses in order to conceal their identity from a public audience. The witnesses would be justified in fearing that a perpetrator following the proceedings in open session could tell from the context of the testimony that the lapse into private session is for the purpose of dealing with allegations of rape in which the perpetrator can expect to be implicated by the witness whom he has recognised as the victim of his past actions. Both witnesses continue to reside in the locations where the alleged crimes were committed. The objective basis of their fear is thus easily and entirely predictable, and entirely predictably established through the three-point test reiterated by the Chamber in its remarks on the 14th of April. The case for Witness 270 is also straightforward. She has expressed such fear that she refuses to testify except in closed session. The unique circumstances she allegedly experienced make her easily identifiable, even under the protection of basic measures. It seems that she has already been targeted by a person who heard her speak publicly about the alleged crimes in another context. Since basic measures do not suffice in the case of Witness 270, she is granted closed session and, as well, a pseudonym. This concludes the reasons for our decision, but I take this opportunity once again to urge the parties to cooperate in matters of protective measures. The parties must know by now what the Chamber will say in each case. That is as it should be. You have a right to expect that the law is clear and that its application is predictable. Tomorrow, it will be the Defence's turn to ask for protective measures for its witnesses, and of course the same rules will apply. Both parties must understand that the Chamber is not prepared to take risks with the security of witnesses in cases where fear has been expressed and where there is an objective basis for the fear. This is not an academic exercise in which hair-splitting technical arguments have any place. The question is instead one of concrete common sense, as in the example considered before, where the perpetrator is assumed to be following the proceedings. Prior to filing written motions for protective measures, the parties should, from now on, explore the possibility of agreement. An oral request to the Chamber might then suffice. Perhaps your cooperation in this regard will be enhanced if I say that the parties by cooperating will not be understood to have waived their right to question the Chamber's approach to protective measures, either in their final briefs or in any appeal from the Chamber's final judgement. This concludes my remarks on the subject of cooperation. Ms. Edgerton, are you ready to start the examination of Witness 84?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I say Witness 84 because we'll not use your name in these proceedings. We'll call you by the number 84. Also, your face cannot be seen by the outside world; neither can your voice be heard directly, that is, your voice is distorted before broadcasted. Apart from that, parts of your testimony that might identify your identity may be given in private session, that is that what you say is not at all conveyed to the public. Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole trust nothing but the truth. I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration of which the text will be handed out to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 84, please be seated. You will first be examined by Ms. Edgerton, counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Edgerton, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we just shift the ELMO away from the witness so that we can see one another, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness 84, now, you're going to be given a sheet of paper with some information on the front. I'd like you to have a look at that sheet of paper and tell us if that's your name and date of birth that appear there and whether that information is correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 84
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd ask that that be filed as the first exhibit, please, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The number will be assigned at a later stage when we have cleaned up the numbering of the previous exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, since this witness's statements will be filed under Rule 89(F), I would ask that we move into closed session, if that's possible, because we'll be talking about the dates in which these statements were taken and that might serve to identify an -- private session, pardon me -- that might serve to be an identifying factor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of April, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.
